summaries.example: Imagine two perfectly matching toy balls. They have the same size, color, and weight. Haecceitism asks whether there could be another complete way the world might be in which the balls keep all those qualities but trade places. The balls would not change in how they look; only which individual is in which place would change.
summaries.summary: Haecceitism is a view about possibilities. It says that a complete possible world might differ from our world only in which individuals occupy particular roles. For example, a different individual might have all the same physical and mental qualities that you have, while you do not exist in that possible world. The world would be qualitatively the same but different in its individual identities. Anti-haecceitism denies this kind of possibility. It says that a change in which individuals exist or which roles they occupy must come with some change in qualities. Philosophers discuss whether examples such as twins swapping roles or identical spheres changing places are genuinely possible. They also ask whether haecceitism fits with views about essential properties, possible worlds, and the identity of things. The entry emphasizes that the answer can depend on how possibilities and possible worlds are understood.
key_ideas: Some philosophers think two possible worlds could have exactly the same qualities but contain different individuals in those roles.
Other philosophers think that if every quality stayed the same, there could not be a further difference about which individual was there.
Haecceitism is about what could have been, not simply about whether special individual properties exist.
Different philosophers may accept some swaps, such as swaps between twins, while rejecting other kinds of swaps.
summaries.why_it_matters: This question helps philosophers understand what makes a thing the very thing it is. It also connects to larger questions about identity, possible worlds, personal identity, physicalism, and space. Thinking about it teaches us that two situations can seem alike in every visible way while still raising a deeper question about who or what is present.

important_terms.definition: A complete way the whole world could have been. Philosophers use this idea to talk about possibilities.
The view that the world could differ in which individuals have which roles, even when all its qualities stay the same.
The view that there cannot be a difference in individuals without some difference in qualities.
A property tied to one particular individual, such as being the person you are. It is sometimes called an individual’s “thisness.”

questions_to_think_about: If two things look and behave exactly alike, what could make them different individuals?
Could two twins trade their places in a story without changing anything else?
Would a different person filling your exact role make a different possible world?
Is imagining something enough to show that it could really happen?

summaries.example: Suppose a possible world contains two qualitatively indiscernible spheres: they have the same mass, shape, color, and relations to everything else. One proposal says there could be another maximal possibility in which the same qualitative arrangement holds but the individual spheres have exchanged their spatial roles. This would be a haecceitistic difference: no qualitative fact changes, but a non-qualitative fact about which individual occupies which role does.
summaries.summary: Haecceitism is a modal thesis: it concerns what could have been. In its central form, it says that there are distinct maximal possibilities that agree in their qualitative features but differ in non-qualitative features, especially which particular individuals occupy those features. A world in which one individual is replaced by a qualitatively identical counterpart, or in which twins exchange their qualitative roles, would therefore differ haecceitistically from actuality. Anti-haecceitism denies that such differences are possible. The entry stresses that no formulation is entirely neutral about the metaphysics of possibilities. Modalists avoid quantifying over possible worlds; other views quantify over maximal possibilities; and possible-world theories differ over whether worlds are abstract representations or concrete realities. In Lewisian modal realism, counterpart theory and qualitative supervenience create a special treatment: haecceitistic possibilities can be represented without adding distinct qualitatively indiscernible worlds. The debate also concerns haecceities, individual essences, and essentialism. Haecceitism does not simply mean that haecceities exist, and even hyperessentialism does not automatically eliminate replacement possibilities involving non-actual individuals. Arguments for the view include conceivability arguments and Chisholm’s Paradox, which uses a sequence of small possible changes to reach a role-swapping result. Arguments against it question whether bare identity facts are intelligible and whether principles about indiscernibility support anti-haecceitism. The entry also examines restricted forms of haecceitism and connections to quidditism, personal identity, physicalism, spacetime, and philosophy of language.
key_ideas: Haecceitism concerns differences between maximal possibilities that are qualitative duplicates but differ in non-qualitative facts about individuals.
Its formulation is controversial because it depends on one’s account of modality, possibilities, and possible worlds.
Haecceitism is distinct from realism about haecceities: one can accept the modal thesis without treating haecceities as properties, or accept haecities while rejecting the modal thesis.
Essentialism restricts some haecceitistic possibilities, but even hyperessentialism may leave open replacement scenarios involving entirely different individuals.
Arguments for haecceitism appeal to conceivability and Chisholm’s Paradox; arguments against it appeal to unexplained identity facts and versions of the Identity of Indiscernibles.

In Lewis’s framework, a single possible world can represent multiple haecceitistically different possibilities, a position often called “cheap haecceitism,” rather than requiring a one-to-one match between worlds and maximal possibilities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Haecceitism tests whether qualitative information completely determines reality. If it is true, a full description of all qualities may still leave open which individuals exist or which individuals occupy particular roles. That possibility affects theories of identity, essence, and the structure of possible worlds. It also matters in debates about personal identity, physical explanation, spacetime models, and the meaning of referring to individuals. Because the issue depends on background theories of modality and ontology, it illustrates how a seemingly simple question about “swapping places” can expose deep assumptions about what makes a possibility distinct.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that distinct maximal possibilities can agree in all qualitative respects while differing in which individuals occupy or instantiate those roles.
The thesis that no maximal possibilities differ only in non-qualitative respects; a qualitative difference must accompany any such difference.
A total way the entire world could have been, rather than a partial possibility concerning only one fact or object.
A property or relation tied to particular individuals, such as being identical with Socrates or being five feet from Napoleon.
A property that does not depend on any particular individual, such as having a certain mass, on the standard examples used in the debate.
An individual-specific “thisness,” often treated as a property uniquely associated with one individual.
The view that an individual has some properties necessarily, so it could not exist without having them.
A view of possible worlds on which worlds are concrete, complete entities, and individuals belong to only one world; de re possibility is explained through counterpart relations.

questions_to_think_about: Does conceiving of two individuals swapping qualitative roles provide good evidence that such a possibility is metaphysically genuine?
Would the Identity of Indiscernibles rule out haecceitism, or does that depend on whether it applies to objects, worlds, or possibilities?
Can identity facts be fundamental, or must they be explained by qualitative facts?
Does a strong essentialist view reject all haecceitistic differences, or only those in which an individual changes its qualitative role?
Should haecceitism be accepted uniformly, or only for restricted domains such as pairs of twins?

summaries.example: Picture two identical-looking twins, Alex and Jamie. In the actual world, Alex is born first. Now imagine a complete possible world where Jamie is born first and Alex second, while every other physical and mental detail remains the same. A haecceitist may say this is a genuinely different possibility because the individuals have exchanged roles. An anti-haecceitist may say it is not a different possibility at all unless some qualitative feature also changes.
summaries.summary: Haecceitism is the view that two complete ways the world could have been may match in every qualitative respect yet differ in which individuals occupy those roles. A familiar illustration is a world where two twins exchange their qualitative positions, such as birth order, without any other difference. Another is a world where a different individual has all of your physical and mental qualities while you do not exist. Anti-haecceitism rejects these as genuine differences: if all qualitative facts are fixed, there is no further possibility left about individual identity. The debate is more complicated than simply asking whether “thisnesses” exist. Haecceitism is a claim about modality, or what is possible, and it can be accepted or rejected under different theories of possible worlds. Some philosophers describe possibilities without worlds; others treat worlds as abstract representations; still others treat them as concrete realities. Essentialism affects the debate by limiting what an individual could be like, but it does not by itself rule out every replacement possibility. Supporters appeal to what seems imaginable and to Chisholm’s Paradox, where a chain of small changes appears to lead to two people trading their qualitative roles. Critics argue that haecceitism would require unexplained “bare” facts about identity, or that suitable forms of the Identity of Indiscernibles support anti-haecceitism. Some philosophers accept only restricted kinds of haecceitistic differences.
key_ideas: The main disagreement is whether identity differences can exist without qualitative differences.
A haecceitistic possibility might involve replacing one individual with another duplicate or swapping the roles of two individuals.
Haecceitism is not identical to the claim that haecceities, or individual “thisnesses,” are real properties.
Possible-world theories disagree about what worlds are, so the best definition of haecceitism can depend on one’s larger theory.
Arguments for haecceitism use imagination and gradual changes; arguments against it question unexplained identity differences and some versions of the Identity of Indiscernibles.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue asks whether a complete list of qualities tells us everything about reality. If it does not, then identity may add something that qualities cannot capture. This affects theories of possible worlds, personal identity, essential properties, and the role of individuals in science and metaphysics. Learning the debate also helps distinguish two questions that are often confused: whether special properties tied to individuals exist, and whether worlds can differ only in which individuals have which properties.

important_terms.definition: A theory about what could be different even when all observable or qualitative features remain unchanged.
The opposing theory that there are no complete possibilities differing only in which individuals fill which roles.
A complete description of one way the entire world might have been.
A property belonging to a particular individual, such as being identical to one named person.
A feature that can be described without referring to a particular individual, such as shape, mass, or color in standard examples.
A feature that refers to or depends on a particular individual, such as being next to a certain person.
The view that some properties are necessary for an individual to be the individual it is.

questions_to_think_about: If Alex and Jamie switch birth order but nothing qualitative changes, has the world really changed?
Could a person fail to exist while a perfect qualitative duplicate takes that person’s place?
Does having an individual essence prevent that individual from switching roles with someone else?
Why might someone think that identity facts need an explanation?
Can a theory accept twin-swapping possibilities while rejecting swaps between very different kinds of things?
